sectionsContent.title: The Bohr Model
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe an electron's energy level in Bohr's model and name the ground state, the excited state and ionization.

notes: *In Bohr's model, an electron stays in a specific energy level, labeled with the letter {{n}}.
The first three levels are n = {{1}}, n = {{2}} and n = {{3}}.
*Quantized means {{set amounts}}. An electron can move between levels but cannot stay {{halfway}} between them.
Today's model uses orbitals to show where electrons are likely to be, their {{probability}}. Electrons do not follow fixed {{circular paths}}.
The higher energy levels are {{closer together}} in energy.

rows: The {{lowest}} energy level. For hydrogen, this is n = {{1}}.
The electron has {{gained energy}} and moved above n = 1.
The electron gains enough energy to {{leave the atom}}.

diagram.label: SKETCH AND LABEL — HYDROGEN ENERGY LEVELS
diagram.caption: Draw n = 1 to n = 4 as horizontal lines, closer together as n rises. Mark the ionization limit.
labels: Lowest line, n = 1, the ground state
n = 2 line, above the ground state
Lines bunch together at higher n

summary: In Bohr's model an electron sits in a set energy level called {{n}}.
Energy comes in set amounts, so it is {{quantized}}.
The lowest level is the {{ground}} state; a higher level is an {{excited}} state.
Enough energy removes the electron entirely, which is {{ionization}}.
selfCheck: I can name n = 1 for hydrogen as the ground state.
I can say how today's model differs from Bohr's circles.

sectionsContent.title: Energy Levels, Sublevels & Orbitals
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can state how many sublevels, orbitals and electrons each energy level holds.

cues: The four-step chain from level to electron
notes: Levels have smaller sections called {{sublevels}}. Sublevels contain {{orbitals}}.
*Level → {{sublevel}} → {{orbital}} → {{electrons}}
*An orbital is a region where an electron is {{likely}} to be.
Each shape is ONE orbital. Any orbital can hold up to {{2}} electrons.

cues: Rule linking level number to sublevels
notes: The level number tells you how many {{sublevels}} it has.

cues: Table — orbitals and electrons per sublevel
notes: Each orbital holds 2 electrons. Count the orbitals to find the total.
*A whole level has {{n²}} orbitals and room for up to {{2n²}} electrons.
The width of each block tells you how many electrons its sublevel can hold.
He is 1s², but it is placed in group {{18}}.
In potassium and calcium, {{4s}} fills before {{3d}}.
Sublevels in n = 3: {{3s, 3p and 3d}}
Electrons in 4f: {{14}}, from {{7}} orbitals × 2
Orbitals in n = 4: {{16}}, from n² = 4²
For n = 3: {{9}} orbitals and a maximum of {{18}} electrons

summary: A level contains {{sublevels}}, a sublevel contains {{orbitals}}, and an orbital holds up to {{2}} electrons.
Capacities are s = {{2}}, p = {{6}}, d = {{10}} and f = {{14}}.
Level n holds up to {{2n²}} electrons in {{n²}} orbitals.
selfCheck: I can list the sublevels in any level up to n = 4.
I can give the electron capacity of s, p, d and f.
I can use n² and 2n² for a whole level.

sectionsContent.title: Electron Configurations
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can write longhand and noble-gas configurations, draw orbital diagrams with Pauli and Hund, and name the Cr and Cu exceptions.

notes: *An electron configuration shows {{where the electrons go}}.
{{Three}} rules help us fill the orbitals: {{Aufbau}}, {{Pauli}} and {{Hund}}.
Example: 2p⁴ means {{four}} electrons in the {{2p}} sublevel.
*For a neutral atom, add the small raised numbers. The total equals the {{atomic number}}.
*Fill the {{lowest}}-energy spaces first. Follow each diagonal arrow.
*One orbital holds {{2}} electrons, and their arrows must point {{opposite}} ways.
Helium has 2 electrons. Both fit in the {{1s}} orbital.
One box = one orbital. One arrow = one electron.

rows.notesLabel: HUND: ONE IN EACH BEFORE PAIRING
notes: *For boxes in the same sublevel, put {{one}} electron in each before making pairs.
The first arrows all point {{up}}. Single electrons in these boxes have the {{same}} spin.
Oxygen starts a pair: the {{fourth}} 2p electron pairs up in one box.
A neutral oxygen atom has {{8}} electrons.
*Full configuration: {{1s² 2s² 2p⁴}}
Unpaired electrons: {{2}}
Ar has {{18}} electrons.
*Ar: {{1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶}}
Check: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = {{18}}. Argon has a full outer s and p.
*Find the matching first 18 electrons, then replace that part with {{[Ar]}}.
Germanium has {{32}} electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p²
Shorthand for Ge: {{[Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p²}}
[Ar] covers {{18}} electrons. Keep the other {{14}}. Total: {{32}}.
Iron has {{26}} electrons. [Ar] already covers the first {{18}}.
26 − 18 = {{8}} electrons left to place.
An arrow without a partner is an unpaired electron. Fe has {{4}} unpaired.
Count the electrons inside [Ar] first, then fill 4s before 3d.
Bromine: {{[Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵}}, and 18 + 2 + 10 + 5 = {{35}}
Longhand and shorthand show the {{same}} arrangement.

rows.notesLabel: WATCH OUT FOR CHROMIUM AND COPPER
notes: These two atoms do not follow the simple filling pattern exactly.
*Their 4s and 3d energies are {{close}}. The actual arrangement has {{less}} total energy.
P, atomic number 15: {{1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³}}
S, atomic number 16: {{[Ne] 3s² 3p⁴}}, with 3p drawn as {{[↑↓] [↑] [↑]}}
Potassium, [Ar] 3d¹ corrected: {{[Ar] 4s¹}}, because {{4s}} fills first.

cues: Nitrogen error and the rule broken
Neon error and the rule broken
notes: Nitrogen's wrong 2p³ diagram breaks {{Hund's}} rule. Correct 2p³: {{one up arrow in each of the three boxes}}.
Neon's wrong 2s² diagram breaks {{Pauli's}} rule. Correct 2s²: {{one up arrow and one down arrow}}.

summary: Aufbau means fill the {{lowest}}-energy sublevel first.
Pauli means an orbital holds {{2}} electrons with {{opposite}} spins.
Hund means put {{one}} electron in each box of a sublevel before {{pairing}}.
Noble-gas shorthand swaps the inner electrons for the matching {{noble gas}} in brackets.
Chromium and copper move one electron from {{4s}} into {{3d}}.
selfCheck: I can write a full configuration and check the total against the atomic number.
I can write a noble-gas shorthand configuration.
I can draw an orbital diagram and count unpaired electrons.
I can name the rule broken in a wrong diagram.

sectionsContent.title: Electron Stability & Valence Electrons
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can count valence electrons, count electrons in an ion and predict the ion an atom forms.

notes: *Valence electrons are the {{outer}} electrons. For the main groups, look for the {{highest}} level number.
Chlorine: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵. Inner electrons: {{[Ne]}}, {{10}} electrons close to the nucleus.
Outer electrons: {{3s² 3p⁵}}, which is {{7}} electrons in the outer level, n = {{3}}.
Noble gases have full outer levels. Usually that is {{8}} electrons. Helium has {{2}}.

rows.notesLabel: USE THE GROUP TO COUNT OUTER ELECTRONS
notes: Main groups are groups {{1}}, {{2}} and {{13–18}}.
Helium is the exception. It has {{2}} outer electrons.

cues: Cation and anion, with an example each
notes: Lose electrons and the charge becomes {{positive}}. Gain them and it becomes {{negative}}.
Cation: loses electrons. Na → Na^+^ + e^−^, and 11 − 1 = {{10}} electrons. Na^+^ has the {{[Ne]}} arrangement.
Anion: gains electrons. Cl + e^−^ → Cl^−^, and 17 + 1 = {{18}} electrons. Cl^−^ has the {{[Ar]}} arrangement.
*Protons stay the same. Electrons = {{atomic number − charge}}.

cues: Table — group, valence and common charge
notes: Many atoms gain or lose a few electrons to get a full outer level. These are common charges for simple ions.

cues: Table — Mg, Al, S, Br with change, ion and noble gas
notes: For each atom, record the outer electron count, the change, the ion and the matching noble gas.
*The outer {{s}} electrons leave before the {{d}} electrons.
{{4s}} fills before 3d, but the {{4s}} electrons leave first when these ions form.

cues: Reason they are still different elements
notes: *Isoelectronic means the same {{electron count}} and arrangement.
With 10 electrons: O^2−^, {{F^−^}}, {{Ne}}, {{Na^+^}} and {{Mg^2+^}}. Arrangement: {{1s² 2s² 2p⁶}}
Their {{proton}} counts are different, so they are still different elements.

summary: Valence electrons are the {{outer}} electrons, and a main-group atom's count matches its {{group}}.
Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a full outer level like a {{noble gas}}.
Metals tend to form {{cations}} and nonmetals tend to form {{anions}}.
Transition metals lose their {{4s}} electrons before their {{3d}} electrons.
Isoelectronic species share the same number of {{electrons}}.
selfCheck: I can find valence electrons from the group number.
I can count electrons in an ion.
I can name the common charge for groups 1, 2, 13, 15, 16 and 17.
I can write a transition-metal ion configuration.

sectionsContent.title: Atomic & Electron Spectra
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can connect electron drops between energy levels to the colors of light atoms give off, and I can record the hydrogen and flame-test data.

cues: Absorption, with direction of the electron
Emission, with direction of the electron
notes: *A photon is a small packet of {{light energy}}.
Absorption (energy in): the electron takes in a photon and moves {{up}} to a higher level.
Emission (light out): the electron {{drops}} to a lower level and gives off a photon.
*The photon's energy equals the {{gap}} between the two levels.

rows.notesLabel: WHICH DROP RELEASES THE MOST ENERGY
notes: Drops compared: A, n = 4 → 2.  B, n = 3 → 2.  C, n = 2 → 1.
Largest gap of these three: drop {{C}}, n = {{2 → 1}}.
*Shorter waves have {{higher}} frequency (more waves each second) and {{more}} energy.
Visible light is about {{400–700}} nm. A violet photon has {{more}} energy than a red one.
A spectrum shows the different {{wavelengths}} of light.
Emission and absorption spectra have bright or dark {{lines}} at specific wavelengths.

cues: Three steps that produce the light
notes: Each element has its own pattern of light.
Step 1, add energy: an electron moves to a {{higher}} level.
Step 2, give off light: the electron drops and releases a {{photon}}.
Step 3, look at the lines: the pattern shows which {{element}} made the light.
*Only certain energy gaps are possible, so only certain {{colors}} appear.
All four drops finish at n = {{2}}.
The {{6 → 2}} drop gives off the most energy of these four. Its wavelength is the {{shortest}}.
Heat gives electrons {{energy}}. As they drop back down, they give off {{light}}.
Sodium gives a {{yellow}} flame and potassium gives a {{lilac}} flame.
*Flame color is a clue. It cannot identify {{every}} substance on its own.
Hydrogen emits only certain wavelengths because only specific {{energy gaps}} are allowed, so only specific photon energies are emitted.
A d sublevel holds {{10}} electrons in {{5}} orbitals.
S: {{[Ne] 3s² 3p⁴}}. {{Two}} electrons are unpaired.
Fe becoming Fe^3+^: the two {{4s}} electrons leave first, then one {{3d}} electron, giving {{[Ar] 3d⁵}}.
{{410}} nm has the higher energy because its wavelength is {{shorter}}.

summary: An electron that gains energy moves {{up}} a level, and an electron that drops gives off a {{photon}}.
The photon's energy equals the {{gap}} between the two levels.
Shorter wavelength means {{higher}} energy, so violet has more energy than {{red}}.
Each element's lines are a fingerprint because only certain {{energy gaps}} exist.
selfCheck: I can say what absorption and emission do to an electron.
I can rank photons by wavelength and energy.
I can list the four visible hydrogen lines.
I can match a flame color to its ion.
